name: Battle of Manzikert
info: On 26 August 1071 the Seljuk army of Alp Arslan defeated the Byzantine army of Romanos IV Diogenes near Manzikert in eastern Anatolia and captured the emperor, and civil strife in Byzantium followed.

facts.place: Near Manzikert, in the theme of Iberia, modern Malazgirt in Muş Province, eastern Turkey
facts.sides: The Byzantine Empire under the emperor Romanos IV Diogenes, with a host of around 40,000 men before it was divided; the Seljuk Empire under the sultan Alp Arslan, with allies and 30,000 cavalry from Aleppo and Mosul, joined by a force of Kurdish fighters estimated at 10,000 sent by the Marwanid emir
facts.outcome: The Byzantine army was routed and Romanos IV was wounded and taken prisoner. After a week he was released on agreed terms, but he was soon deposed and blinded in a civil war.

t: Romanos had split his army before the battle, and the Byzantine reserve under Andronikos Doukas withdrew to the camp instead of covering the retreat, which left the rest of the line exposed.

Modern scholars estimate that Byzantine losses were relatively low and that many units fought elsewhere within a few months. The lasting damage came from the civil war that followed, which the Seljuks used to their advantage.
Later Byzantine writers called Manzikert a disaster and greatly exaggerated the numbers of troops and casualties; Delbrück thought the battle's importance exaggerated.
dyk: It was the only time a Byzantine emperor became the prisoner of a Muslim commander, and the first time since Valerian that a Roman emperor was captured alive by an enemy force.
ev: Constantine IX disbands the "Iberian Army", which Skylitzes puts at 50,000 men
Alp Arslan attacks the theme of Iberia and takes Ani after a siege of 25 days
Romanos IV Diogenes takes power and begins two major campaigns against the Seljuks and their Mirdasid allies
Romanos's army reaches Theodosiopolis and the march continues towards Lake Van
Romanos takes Manzikert and his army is defeated by the Seljuks nearby
Romanos is released after a week, loses three battles to the Doukas family, and is deposed and blinded
The Seljuks establish their capital at Nikaea
The First Crusade begins as a western response to the Byzantine emperor's call for help

sections.background:
The Byzantine Empire had remained strong in the early Middle Ages, but it began to decline under the militarily incompetent Constantine IX Monomachos and again under Constantine X Doukas. A brief two-year period of reform under Isaac I Komnenos only delayed the decay of the army. About 1053 Constantine IX disbanded what the historian John Skylitzes called the "Iberian Army", of 50,000 men. Skylitzes' contemporaries Michael Attaleiates and Kekaumenos agree that this did catastrophic harm to the empire's eastern defences. A truce with the Seljuks lasted until 1064, when a large army under Alp Arslan attacked the theme of Iberia and took Ani after a siege of 25 days.

In 1068 Romanos IV Diogenes took power and, after some military reforms, conducted two major campaigns against the Seljuks and their Mirdasid allies. He retook Hierapolis in 1068 and chased Turkoman armies that were raiding across Anatolia, with limited success, but he could not win a decisive victory in 1069. In 1069 or 1070 Manuel Komnenos led an expedition and was defeated at Sebasteia by Arisighi, Alp Arslan's brother-in-law, who then joined the Byzantines and gave them information about Seljuk politics and tactics.

Alp Arslan failed to capture Edessa after a lengthy siege and turned to besiege Aleppo. Romanos saw an opportunity to lead a large army into Armenia and recover the lost fortresses before the Seljuks could respond.
sections.forces:
With Romanos went Andronikos Doukas, son of his rival John Doukas. The army had about 5,000 professional troops from the western provinces and probably about as many from the eastern provinces, drawn from the central field army, the tagmata. The rear guard under Doukas was largely made up of the private retinues and peasant levies of the border lords. The host also held 500 Frankish and Norman mercenaries under Roussel de Bailleul, Uz, Pecheneg and Bulgarian mercenaries, infantry under the Duke of Antioch, a Georgian and Armenian contingent and some, but not all, of the Varangian Guard, around 40,000 men in total. The provincial troops had declined in number because the government diverted funds to mercenaries, who were judged less likely to be involved in politics and could be disbanded after use.

Alp Arslan was already in the area with allies and 30,000 cavalry from Aleppo and Mosul. The Marwanid emir Nizam al-Din ibn Nasr al-Dawla sent a force of Kurdish fighters estimated at 10,000. Alp Arslan's scouts knew where Romanos was, while Romanos did not know where his opponent was.

Romanos then ordered Joseph Tarchaniotes to take some of the regular troops and the Varangians, with the Pechenegs and Franks, to Khliat, while he marched on Manzikert. This left about 20,000 men in each half. What became of Tarchaniotes's force is unknown.
sections.course:
Romanos, unaware that Tarchaniotes was gone, took Manzikert on 23 August, and the Seljuks answered with horse archers. The next day foraging parties under Bryennios found the main Seljuk force and fell back, and the cavalry Romanos sent under the Armenian general Basilakes was routed and Basilakes captured. On 25 August some of Romanos's Turkic mercenaries met their Seljuk kin and deserted, and Romanos rejected a Seljuk peace emissary.

On the morning of 26 August Alp Arslan, in a white robe like a funeral shroud, made a speech to his army. The Byzantines formed up with Bryennios on the left, Theodore Alyates on the right, the emperor in the centre and Andronikos Doukas leading the reserve in the rear. The Seljuks stood in a crescent about four kilometres away. Their horse archers attacked as the Byzantines advanced, the centre of the crescent giving way while the wings moved round the Byzantine troops. The Byzantines captured Alp Arslan's camp by the end of the afternoon, but the wings almost broke up when units tried to force a pitched battle and the Seljuk cavalry simply disengaged.

Romanos ordered a withdrawal by nightfall. The right wing misunderstood it, and Doukas ignored the order to cover the retreat and marched to the camp. The Seljuks attacked, routed the right wing, then the left under Bryennios, and encircled the remnants of the centre, including the emperor and the Varangian Guard. Romanos was wounded and taken prisoner.
sections.aftermath:
When Romanos was brought before Alp Arslan, the sultan at first did not believe that the bloodied man was the emperor. After learning who he was, he placed his boot on Romanos's neck and made him kiss the ground, a traditional symbolic gesture, then treated him with considerable kindness and offered again the peace terms he had offered before the battle. Romanos stayed a captive for a week and ate at the sultan's table while terms were agreed: Antioch, Edessa, Hierapolis and Manzikert were to be surrendered. The sultan's demand of 10 million gold pieces as ransom was judged too high and was reduced to 1.5 million as an initial payment followed by 360,000 a year, with a marriage alliance between the sultan's son and Romanos's daughter.

Doukas had escaped without casualties and went back to Constantinople, where he led a coup against Romanos and proclaimed his cousin Michael VII basileus. The Seljuks did not pursue the fleeing Byzantines nor retake Manzikert at this point. All the Byzantine commanders survived and most prisoners were later released. The most serious material loss was the emperor's baggage train.

Romanos was defeated three times in battle by the Doukas family, deposed, blinded and exiled to the island of Proti, and died soon after of an infection caused by the blinding.
sections.sources:
Much of what is known comes from Byzantine writers, among them Michael Attaleiates, John Skylitzes and Kekaumenos, who were contemporaries or near contemporaries, and from Anna Komnene, writing a few decades after the battle. Islamic sources add details, and Ibn al-Adim reports what Romanos said before Alp Arslan, that he blamed raids by Rashid al-Dawla Mahmud into Byzantine territory for his interventions in Muslim territories.

The sources disagree in places. According to Islamic sources Alp Arslan smashed the army sent off with Tarchaniotes, but Byzantine sources do not mention any such encounter, and Attaleiates suggests Tarchaniotes fled at the sight of the sultan, an event that seems unlikely given the general's reputation. Some authors suppose the Armenians were the first to flee, while others say Armenian infantry resisted stoutly and did not abandon the emperor.

Later Byzantine historians looked back on the day as a disaster and the start of the empire's decline, and later sources greatly exaggerated the numbers of troops and casualties. Modern scholars have revised the older picture of a massacre. Andrew Holt, in a 2022 anthology, argues that Romanos was largely to blame, citing his decision to give Andronikos so large a command, his division of his forces on poor intelligence and the poor leadership and discipline of his troops.
sections.legacy:
In simplest terms the defeat meant the loss of the empire's Anatolian heartland. John Julius Norwich calls it "its death blow" and the greatest disaster in the empire's seven and a half centuries, and Steven Runciman calls it the most decisive disaster in Byzantine history. Thomas Asbridge says historians no longer consider it an utterly cataclysmic reversal, though still a stinging setback. Delbrück considers its importance exaggerated, but the evidence shows it left the empire unable to put an effective army into the field for many years.

The battle was the first link in a chain: intrigues for the throne, Romanos's fate, and Roussel de Bailleul's attempt to carve out a kingdom in Galatia with 3,000 Frankish, Norman and German mercenaries. By 1080 the Seljuk Turks had gained an area of 78,000 square kilometres, and they made Nikaea their capital in 1077. It took three decades of internal strife before Alexius I restored stability. The First Crusade of 1095 began as a western response to the Byzantine emperor's call for help after the loss of Anatolia. The Battle of Myriokephalon has been compared to it.

Norman soldiers who had served in Byzantine armies spread tales of the defeat that likely inspired an episode in the Chanson de Roland. In Turkey the Çamlıca Mosque's minarets span 107.1 metres, a measurement that refers to 1071, and the 1000th anniversary of the battle is one of the targets announced in 2018 by the ruling AKP.

summary: At Manzikert on 26 August 1071 the Seljuk army under Alp Arslan routed a Byzantine host led by the emperor Romanos IV Diogenes, who was captured. Byzantine losses were relatively low by modern estimates, but civil war followed and the Seljuks gained much of Anatolia.

notes: The article's strengths: 40,000 is its figure for the whole Byzantine host before the split; it gives no Seljuk total beyond 30,000 cavalry plus 10,000 Kurdish fighters. No casualty figures are given; it says only that modern scholars estimate losses were relatively low and later sources exaggerated.
Tarchaniotes: Islamic sources say Alp Arslan smashed his force, Byzantine sources are silent, Attaleiates says he fled; the article says it is unknown what happened.

The article contradicts itself slightly: the lead says Turkification of Anatolia followed, and calls the battle decisive, while the aftermath says it did not directly change the balance of power and that Delbrück thinks its importance exaggerated; both are given attributed.

The article says Romanos was captive for a week and was released 'a week later'; it also says the Byzantine army regrouped at Dokeia. Doukas's coup is placed in Constantinople at once; the deposition timeline is not dated in the article.
The ev entry 1071 for Romanos's deposition has no month in the article.
The article's date for Hierapolis is 1068 and it says Romanos failed to win a decisive victory in 1069; 'In 1069 or 1070' for Manuel Komnenos is as given.

Left out: Arisighi's refusal at Chrysopolis and Afshin Bey's raids, the Armenian general's name detail, Anna Komnene's quotation, Paul K. Davis's verdict, Alp Arslan's reported reaction details, the question of the Roussel episode's Seljuk ransom.
